{{Short description|Mathematical function}}
{{distinguish|Mittag-Leffler polynomials}}
[[File:MittagLeffler GaussToLorentz.gif|thumb|right|300px|The Mittag-Leffler function can be used to interpolate continuously between a Gaussian and a Lorentzian function.]]

In [[mathematics]],  the '''Mittag-Leffler functions''' are a family of [[special function]]s. They are complex-valued functions of a complex argument ''z'', and moreover depend on one or two complex parameters.

The '''one-parameter Mittag-Leffler function''', introduced by [[Gösta Mittag-Leffler]] in 1903,<ref>Mittag-Leffler, M.G.: Sur la nouvelle fonction E(x). C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 137, 554–558 (1903), and several more papers in the following years.</ref><ref name=":0">Haubold, H J and Mathai, A M and Saxena, R K, [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1155/2011/298628 J Appl Math 2011, 298628]</ref> can be defined by the Maclaurin series

:<math>E_{\alpha} (z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{z^k}{\Gamma(\alpha k + 1)},</math>

where <math>\Gamma(x) </math> is the [[gamma function]], and <math>\alpha</math> is a complex parameter with <math>\operatorname{Re}\left(\alpha \right)> 0</math>.

The '''two-parameter Mittag-Leffler function''', introduced by Wiman in 1905,<ref>Anders Wiman, Über den Fundamentalsatz in der Teorie [sic] der Funktionen <math>E_a(x)</math>, Acta Math 29, 191-201 (1905).</ref><ref name=":0"/> is occasionally called the '''generalized Mittag-Leffler function'''. It has an additional complex parameter <math>\beta</math>, and may be defined by the series<ref name=":0"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Mittag-LefflerFunction.html|title=Mittag-Leffler Function|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en|access-date=2019-09-11}}</ref>

:<math>E_{\alpha, \beta} (z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{z^k}{\Gamma(\alpha k + \beta)},</math>

When <math>\beta=1</math>, the one-parameter function <math>E_\alpha = E_{\alpha,1}</math> is recovered.

In the case <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are real and positive, the series converges for all values of the argument <math>z</math>, so the Mittag-Leffler function is an [[entire function]]. This class of functions are important in the theory of the [[fractional calculus]].

See below for [[#Three-parameter generalizations|three-parameter generalizations]].

==Some basic properties==

For <math>\alpha >0 </math>, the Mittag-Leffler function <math>E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)</math> is an entire function of [[Entire function#Order and type|order]] <math>1/\alpha</math>, and [[Entire function#Order and type|type]] <math>1</math> for any value of <math>\beta</math>. In some sense, the Mittag-Leffler function is the simplest entire function of its order. The [[indicator function (complex analysis)|indicator function]] of <math>E_{\alpha}(z)</math> is<ref name="Cartwright">{{cite book |last1=Cartwright|first1=M. L. |title=Integral Functions |date=1962 |publisher=Cambridge Univ. Press |isbn=052104586X}}</ref>{{rp|p=50}}
<math display="block">h_{E_\alpha}(\theta)=\begin{cases}\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{\alpha}\right),&\text{for }|\theta|\le\frac 1 2 \alpha\pi;\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}</math>
This result actually holds for <math>\beta\neq1</math> as well with some restrictions on <math>\beta</math> when <math>\alpha=1</math>.<ref name="Gorenfloetal" />{{rp|p=67}}

The Mittag-Leffler function satisfies the recurrence property (Theorem 5.1 of <ref name=":0" />)

:<math>E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\frac{1}{z}E_{\alpha,\beta-\alpha}(z)-\frac{1}{z \Gamma(\beta-\alpha)},</math>
from which the following [[asymptotic expansion]] holds : for <math>0<\alpha<2</math> and <math>\mu</math> real such that  
<math>\frac{\pi\alpha}{2} < \mu < \min(\pi, \pi\alpha)</math> then for all <math>N\in\mathbb{N}^*, N\neq 1</math>, we can show the following asymptotic expansions (Section 6. of <ref name=":0" />):

-as <math>\,|z|\to+\infty, |\text{arg}(z)|\leq \mu</math>:

:<math>E_{\alpha}(z) = \frac{1}{\alpha} \exp(z^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}) - \sum\limits_{k=1}^{N} \frac{1}{z^k\, \Gamma(1-\alpha k)} + O\left(\frac{1}{z^{N+1}}\right)</math>,

-and as <math>\,|z|\to+\infty, \mu\leq|\text{arg}(z)|\leq\pi</math>:

:<math>E_{\alpha}(z) = - \sum\limits_{k=1}^N \frac{1}{z^k\Gamma(1-\alpha k)} + O\left(\frac{1}{z^{N+1}}\right)</math>.

A simpler estimate that can often be useful is given, thanks to the fact that the order and type of <math>E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)</math> is <math>1/\alpha</math> and <math>1</math>, respectively:<ref name="Gorenfloetal" />{{rp|p=62}}
:<math>|E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)|\le C\exp\left(\sigma|z|^{1/\alpha}\right)</math>
for any positive <math>C</math> and any <math>\sigma>1</math>.

==Special cases==

For <math>\alpha=0</math>, the series above equals the [[Taylor series|Taylor expansion]] of the [[geometric series]] and consequently <math>E_{0,\beta}(z)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\frac{1}{1-z}</math>.
 
For <math>\alpha=\tfrac12,1,2</math> we find: (Section 2 of <ref name=":0" />)

[[Error function]]:

:<math>E_{\frac{1}{2}}(z) = \exp(z^2)\operatorname{erfc}(-z).</math>

[[Exponential function]]:
:<math>E_{1}(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{z^k}{\Gamma (k + 1)} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{z^k}{k!} = \exp(z).</math>

[[Hyperbolic functions]]:
:<math>E_{2}(z) = \cosh(\sqrt{z}), \text{ and } E_{2}(-z^2) = \cos(z).</math>

For <math>\beta=2</math>, we have

:<math>E_{1,2}(z) = \frac{e^z-1}{z},</math>
:<math>E_{2,2}(z) = \frac{\sinh(\sqrt{z})}{\sqrt{z}}.</math>

For <math>\alpha=0,1,2</math>, the integral

:<math>\int_0^z E_{\alpha}(-s^2) \, {\mathrm d}s</math>

gives, respectively: <math>\arctan(z)</math>, <math>\tfrac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\operatorname{erf}(z)</math>,  <math>\sin(z)</math>.

[[Hypergeometric functions]]:

For <math>p\in \mathbb{N}</math> a general formula for a half-integer parameter <math>\frac{p}{2}</math> is
:<math>E_{\frac{p}{2}}(z) = {}_{0}F_{p-1}\bigg(;\frac{1}{p},\frac{2}{p},...,\frac{p-1}{p};\frac{z^2}{p^p}\bigg) + \frac{2^{\frac{p+1}{2}}z}{p!\sqrt{\pi}}{}_{1}F_{2p-1}\bigg(1;\frac{p+2}{2p},\frac{p+3}{2p},...,\frac{3p}{2p};\frac{z^2}{p^p}\bigg)</math><ref name="hypergeo" />
[[Incomplete gamma function]]:

For <math>p\in \mathbb{N}-\{1\}</math>
:<math>E_{\frac{1}{p}}(z^{\frac{1}{p}}) = e^{z} \bigg[1+\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}\frac{\gamma(1-\frac{n}{p},z)}{\Gamma(1-\frac{n}{p})}\bigg]</math><ref name = "incgamma"/>
where <math>\gamma(x,y)</math> is the incomplete gamma function.

==Mittag-Leffler's integral representation==
The integral representation of the Mittag-Leffler function is (Section 6 of <ref name=":0" />)

:<math>E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C \frac{t^{\alpha-\beta}e^t}{t^\alpha-z} \, dt,
\Re(\alpha)>0, \Re(\beta)>0,</math>

where the contour <math>C</math> starts and ends at <math>-\infty</math> and circles around the singularities and branch points of the integrand.

Related to the [[Laplace transform]] and [[Mittag-Leffler summation]] is the expression (Eq (7.5) of <ref name=":0" /> with <math>m=0</math>)

:<math>\int_0^{\infty}e^{-t z} t^{\beta-1} E_{\alpha,\beta}(\pm r\, t^\alpha) \,dt
= \frac{z^{\alpha-\beta}}{z^{\alpha}\mp r},
\Re(z)>0, \Re(\alpha)>0, \Re(\beta)>0.</math>

For <math>\operatorname{Re}(z^{1/\alpha}) < 1</math>, the Mittag-Leffler function satisfies the integral identity

:<math>\frac{1}{1-z} = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-u} E_{\alpha}(z u^{\alpha}) \, du.</math><ref name = "int 1/z"/>
For <math>\alpha > 0</math>, the Mellin [[Barnes integral]] representation using a straight line contour is
:<math>E_{\alpha}(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\gamma-i\infty}^{\gamma+i\infty}\frac{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(1-s)}{\Gamma(1-\alpha s)}(-z)^{-s} ds,|\arg{z}| < \pi </math><ref name = "Barnes"/>
Which can be written in terms of generalized [[Fox–Wright function]] 
:<math>E_{\alpha}(z) = {}_{1}\Psi_{1} \left[ \begin{matrix} (1, 1) \\ (1, \alpha) \end{matrix} \bigg| z \right]</math>
And in terms of [[Fox H-function]]
:<math>E_{\alpha}(z) = H^{1,1}_{1,2}\left[ -z \bigg| \begin{matrix} (0, 1) \\ (0,1),(0, \alpha) \end{matrix} \right]</math>

==Three-parameter generalizations==

One generalization, characterized by three parameters, is

<math>E_{\alpha,\beta}^\gamma(z)=\left ( \frac{1}{\Gamma(\gamma)} \right )\sum\limits_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\Gamma(\gamma + k)z^k}{k! \Gamma(\alpha k + \beta )  },</math>

where <math>\alpha, \beta</math> and <math>\gamma</math> are complex parameters and <math>\Re(\alpha)>0</math>.<ref name="Gorenfloetal">{{Cite book |last1=Gorenflo |first1=Rudolf |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-662-43930-2 |title=Mittag-Leffler Functions, Related Topics and Applications: Theory and Applications |last2=Kilbas |first2=Anatoly A. |last3=Mainardi |first3=Francesco |last4=Rogosin |first4=Sergei V. |date=2014 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-662-43929-6 |series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-43930-2}}</ref>

Another generalization is the [[Prabhakar function]]

<math>E_{\alpha, \beta}^{\gamma}(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(\gamma)_k z^k}{k!\Gamma(\alpha k + \beta)}, </math>

where <math>(\gamma)_k</math> is the [[Pochhammer symbol]].

==Applications of Mittag-Leffler function==
One of the applications of the Mittag-Leffler function is in modeling fractional order viscoelastic materials. Experimental investigations into the time-dependent relaxation behavior of viscoelastic materials are characterized by a very fast decrease of the stress at the beginning of the relaxation process and an extremely slow decay for large times, i.e. it takes a long time to approach a constant asymptotic value. Therefore, many Maxwell elements are required to describe relaxation behavior to sufficient accuracy. This results in a difficult [[optimization problem]] in order to identify the large number of material parameters required. On the other hand, over the years, the concept of fractional derivatives has been introduced into the theory of [[viscoelasticity]]. Among these models, the [[Standard linear solid model|fractional Zener]] model was found to be very effective for predicting the dynamic nature of rubber-like materials using only a small number of material parameters. The solution of the corresponding [[constitutive equation]] leads to a relaxation function of the Mittag-Leffler type. It is defined by the [[power series]] with negative arguments. This function represents all essential properties of the relaxation process under the influence of an arbitrary and continuous signal with a jump at the origin.<ref>Pritz, T. (2003). Five-parameter fractional derivative model for polymeric damping materials. Journal of Sound and Vibration, 265(5), 935-952.</ref><ref>Nonnenmacher, T. F., & Glöckle, W. G. (1991). A fractional model for mechanical stress relaxation. Philosophical magazine letters, 64(2), 89-93.</ref>
